England.difference_en: England Year 1 begins with direct comparison of length, height, mass and capacity before extending into measurement units. China likewise develops measurement through practical comparison and measuring activity.
England.why_en: Comparing quantities before reading scales helps units acquire a real magnitude meaning.
England.classroom_use_en: Compare two objects first, then choose an appropriate tool and unit to measure them.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grade 1 explicitly compares lengths directly and indirectly using a third object.
US.why_en: Indirect comparison moves beyond visual judgement into a transferable quantitative relationship.
US.classroom_use_en: Use a strip of paper as a common reference for two objects that cannot be placed together.

England.difference_en: England Years 1-2 move from practical measurement into standard units such as metres, centimetres, grams, kilograms and litres.
England.why_en: Standard units allow measurements made by different people to be compared and communicated.
England.classroom_use_en: Measure one desk first with hand spans and then in centimetres and discuss why the first result varies between people.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grade 2 explicitly measures with standard length units and compares measurements made using units of different sizes.
US.why_en: Smaller measurement units produce larger numerical counts, which prepares pupils for unit conversion.
US.classroom_use_en: Estimate the same object in metres and centimetres and predict which numerical measure will be larger.

England.difference_en: England progressively uses common metric relationships and conversion across Years 3-6.
England.why_en: The quantity stays the same while the unit changes size; conversion is not only a multiply/divide rule.
England.classroom_use_en: Before converting, ask whether changing to a smaller unit should make the numerical value larger or smaller.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grades 4-5 convert measurement units within a measurement system and use conversions in multi-step problems.
US.why_en: Unit relationships can be represented multiplicatively in tables rather than memorised as isolated rules.
US.classroom_use_en: Use a ratio table for 1 m=100 cm and extend it to several lengths.

England.difference_en: England expects estimation and appropriate unit choice throughout practical measurement work.
England.why_en: A useful estimate is based on internal benchmarks, such as an approximate metre, rather than a random guess.
England.classroom_use_en: Estimate before measuring and compare the estimate with the measured result.

US.difference_en: Common Core measurement work requires appropriate tools/units and reasoning about measurement quantities; estimation can support problem solving and reasonableness.
US.why_en: Unit and magnitude checks can eliminate impossible answers before calculation.
US.classroom_use_en: Choose whether a classroom is more reasonably 8 mm, 8 m or 8 km and justify the unit.

England.difference_en: England progresses from hour/half-hour in Year 1 to five-minute intervals in Year 2 and minute-level time plus 12/24-hour notation in Year 3.
England.why_en: The clock scale becomes more precise while the hour hand continues to move continuously between hour marks.
England.classroom_use_en: For 3:30, ask what both the minute hand and the hour hand are showing.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grade 1 reads hour/half-hour, Grade 2 to five minutes, and Grade 3 solves minute-level interval problems.
US.why_en: Reading a clock and reasoning about elapsed time are related but distinct skills.
US.classroom_use_en: After reading a time, ask where both hands would be ten minutes later.

England.difference_en: England moves from comparing time intervals in Year 2 into duration and event-time problems in Year 3.
England.why_en: Elapsed time is the distance between two times, not simple subtraction of visible clock digits.
England.classroom_use_en: Show 9:45 to 10:20 as 15 minutes to 10:00 plus 20 minutes.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grade 3 explicitly solves elapsed-time problems to the nearest minute and may use number-line diagrams.
US.why_en: A timeline turns duration into a measurable distance and helps with crossing an hour boundary.
US.classroom_use_en: Mark start and end times first, then partition the interval at a convenient hour point.

England.difference_en: England Year 1 explicitly names and sequences days, weeks, months and years and uses dates.
England.why_en: Calendar units are not a uniform base-ten system; month lengths and leap years follow real conventions.
England.classroom_use_en: Use a real calendar for cross-month duration rather than assuming every month has 30 days.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grades 1-6 do not contain a standalone calendar progression comparable with England; primary time standards focus more directly on clocks and elapsed time.
US.why_en: This is a curriculum-organisation difference, not a reason to avoid calendar contexts.
US.classroom_use_en: Use calendar tasks as time-context applications without labelling them as a specific Common Core standard when none exists.

England.difference_en: England Year 1 recognises coin/note values and Year 2 combines different denominations to make equivalent amounts.
England.why_en: The number of coins is not the same as monetary value, making money a useful context for unitising and equivalence.
England.classroom_use_en: Compare five 10-cent coins with two 50-cent coins by value rather than coin count.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grade 2 explicitly solves word problems involving dollars, quarters, dimes, nickels and pennies.
US.why_en: Money provides a practical setting for addition/subtraction and unit values.
US.classroom_use_en: Make the same total with different coin combinations and explain why the values are equivalent.

England.difference_en: England Year 2 onward uses monetary amounts, totals and change in practical problems.
England.why_en: Change is a difference and can be found by subtraction or counting up.
England.classroom_use_en: For a 37-yuan item paid with 50 yuan, compare 50-37 with counting up from 37 to 50.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grade 2 money problems use addition and subtraction for totals and differences; money can then continue as a multi-step context.
US.why_en: Identifying total, amount paid and difference is more reliable than choosing an operation from a keyword.
US.classroom_use_en: Before calculating, state what each monetary amount represents.
